planting.note: Root a stolon plantlet or stem-tip cutting in moist peat-based mix or perlite, then pot up into a shallow container once new leaves form. Best started in spring or summer so the mat of runners fills in before lower-light winter months. Grown indoors year-round as a houseplant.

directions: This cultivar is grown for its quilted, olive-green leaves overlaid with a frosty silver sheen along the veins, a striking contrast to the plain-flowered species, with small orange-red tubular flowers appearing sporadically above the foliage. Grow in bright, indirect light or under fluorescent tubes, since deep shade thins the silvering and hot direct sun scorches the leaves. Pot in a light, humus-rich mix that stays evenly moist but never soggy, and water from below or around the base to avoid spotting the fuzzy foliage. Its trailing stolons make it well suited to a shallow, wide dish or hanging basket, where it roots as it spreads and forms a dense mat over time.
sources: Gesneriad Reference Web — Episcia cupreata cultivars

directions: One of the oldest and most recognizable flame violet cultivars, valued for deeply quilted, chocolate-brown leaves etched with silvery-green veining, set off by small orange-red flowers held just above the foliage. Grow in bright, indirect light, which deepens the brown coloring; too little light shifts the leaves toward plain green. Pot in a loose, well-drained, humus-rich mix and keep it lightly and evenly moist, watering around the base rather than overhead since droplets can spot the velvety leaves. Its runners root readily as they spread, making it easy to fill a shallow dish garden or hanging basket, and older mats benefit from occasional thinning to keep the foliage dense and colorful.

directions: This variegated sport carries pink, cream, and green marbled foliage that is showier but slower-growing and less vigorous than the plain species, with modest orange flowers that take a back seat to the leaf color. Grow in bright, indirect light to hold the pink tones; too much shade fades the variegation back toward solid green, while direct sun scorches the pale patches. Pot in a light, fast-draining, humus-rich mix and keep it evenly moist without letting water sit on the leaves, which are prone to spotting. Because the all-white and palest-pink sectors lack chlorophyll, growth is naturally less vigorous than green-leaved episcias, so give it slightly warmer, more humid conditions and avoid heavy feeding.

planting.note: Root 3-4 inch stem-tip cuttings in moist perlite or a light peat-based mix, then transplant into a hanging basket or pot once rooted. Best propagated in spring or summer for full establishment before winter. Grown indoors year-round as a houseplant.

directions: A popular hybrid prized for its compact, self-branching habit and heavy repeat bloom of hooded, orange-red tubular flowers set against small, thick, glossy dark green leaves. Unlike lankier trailing columneas, 'Chanticleer' mounds and branches on its own with little pinching, making it a good choice for growers who want the goldfish-plant look without constant grooming. Grow in bright, indirect light for the heaviest flowering, and pot in a light, fast-draining, humus-rich mix, letting the top of the mix dry slightly between waterings. Steady warmth and humidity encourage the near-continuous flower flushes this cultivar is known for, while cold drafts and dry air cause bud drop.

planting.note: Root 3-4 inch stem-tip cuttings in moist perlite or a light peat-based mix, then transplant into a hanging basket once rooted. Best propagated in spring or summer for full establishment before winter. Grown indoors year-round as a houseplant.

directions: A vigorous, easy-care hybrid long popular in northern Europe as a hanging houseplant, carrying thick, glossy, succulent-like leaves on long trailing stems studded with hooded orange-red flowers for much of the year. It tolerates the lower indoor humidity of centrally heated homes better than many thinner-leaved columneas, making it a forgiving choice for beginners. Grow in bright, indirect light and pot in a light, fast-draining, humus-rich mix, watering thoroughly and letting the top inch dry before watering again. Display it in a hanging basket where the trailing stems, which can reach several feet, are free to cascade, and pinch tips occasionally to keep growth full rather than leggy.

planting.note: Root 4-6 inch stem-tip cuttings in moist perlite or a light peat-based mix, then move to a hanging basket once new growth shows. Best propagated in spring or summer for full establishment before winter. Grown indoors year-round outside frost-free tropical climates.

directions: Grown as much for its foliage as its flowers, this hybrid carries thick, glossy leaves checkered with dark brown-black mottling over green, resembling tiger or snakeskin markings, with clusters of orange-red flowers emerging from near-black calyces. Grow in bright, indirect light to keep the leaf patterning crisp; low light causes the markings to fade toward plain green. Pot in a chunky, fast-draining epiphytic mix of bark, perlite, and peat, and let the surface dry slightly between waterings, since soggy roots quickly lead to stem rot. Best displayed in a hanging basket where the trailing stems can show off both the patterned upper leaf surface and the flowers, and maintain steady warmth and humidity for the healthiest growth.

planting.note: Root 4-6 inch stem-tip cuttings in moist perlite or a light peat-based mix, then move to a hanging basket once new growth shows. Best propagated in spring or summer for full establishment before winter. Grown indoors year-round outside frost-free tropical climates.

directions: A free-flowering hybrid valued for its compact, well-branched trailing habit and heavy sets of bright red flowers emerging from dark maroon calyces against small, glossy, deep green leaves. Grow in bright, indirect light, since good light is the main driver of bloom count in this genus and low light produces mostly foliage. Pot in a chunky, fast-draining epiphytic mix of bark, perlite, and peat, and water thoroughly, then let the surface dry before watering again to avoid root rot. Pinch stem tips after each round of bloom to encourage further branching, and display it in a hanging basket where the naturally bushy, cascading stems can fill out fully.

planting.note: Root 3-4 inch stem tip cuttings in moist perlite or a light mix, then transplant into a hanging basket once rooted. Best started in spring or summer so trailing stems fill in before lower-light winter months. Grown indoors year-round as a houseplant.

directions: A striking cultivar grown for its near-black, glossy leaves that set off small, waxy, orange pouch-shaped flowers typical of the genus. The dark foliage color develops best in bright, indirect light; in lower light the leaves shift toward ordinary dark green and lose some of their sheen. Pot in a light, fast-draining mix and let the top inch dry between waterings, since the thick leaves store some moisture and the roots dislike sitting wet. Grow in a hanging basket to let the trailing stems cascade, and pinch tips after flowering flushes to keep the plant compact and encourage branching rather than long, bare runners.

planting.note: Root a leaf or stem cutting in moist perlite or a light peat-based mix; small tubers form at the base over several months. Best started in spring or summer for full establishment before winter. Grown indoors year-round as a houseplant.

directions: A compact hybrid gesneriad bred for a neat, mounding rosette of soft, fuzzy leaves and abundant soft yellow, slipper-shaped flowers held just above the foliage. Grow in bright, indirect light or under fluorescent or LED plant lights, since direct sun scorches the hairy leaves while too little light reduces flowering. Pot in a light, well-drained, humus-rich mix and water thoroughly, letting the surface dry slightly before watering again; water at the soil line to avoid spotting the leaves. It forms a small tuber over time and can be rested dry and cool for a few months if growth slows, then started back into growth in spring like other tuberous sinningias.

planting.note: Start dormant scaly rhizomes shallowly in moist, warm potting mix in early to mid spring; growth stalls in cool soil below roughly 70F. Grown as a warm-season houseplant or basket plant, dormant and dry over winter.

directions: One of the oldest and most enduring Achimenes cultivars, prized for its dwarf, mounding habit and profusion of small, deep magenta-pink flowers with a yellow-white throat that nearly cover the foliage at peak bloom. Its compact size makes it well suited to small pots, dish gardens, or the front edge of a mixed basket, unlike taller, lankier achimenes. Grow in bright, indirect light with some protection from hot midday sun, and pot in a light, humus-rich mix kept evenly moist through the growing season. As bloom fades in autumn, gradually withhold water and let the top growth die back, then store the small dormant rhizomes dry and cool until repotting the following spring.
sources: University of Florida IFAS Extension — Gesneriads for indoor flowering

directions: A classic heirloom cultivar bearing soft peachy-pink, flared, tubular flowers with a pale throat over lax, slightly hairy, toothed foliage on semi-trailing stems. Grow in bright, indirect light with protection from hot midday sun, since strong direct light can bleach the delicate flower color. Pot in a light, humus-rich mix that stays evenly moist through the growing season without becoming waterlogged, and provide reasonably high humidity, as dry air tends to brown the leaf edges. Once flowering winds down in fall, gradually reduce water and allow top growth to die back naturally, then store the scaly rhizomes dry and cool until repotting the following spring.
sources: University of Florida IFAS Extension — Gesneriads for indoor flowering
